newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe lending rates fall, firms want more cuts.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe lending rates fall, firms want more cuts.

text.p: Zimbabwean lending rates have fallen below 30 percent for the first time in five years leaving businessmen calling for more cuts and analysts warning of inflationary dangers.

Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of economic and share market analysts Dataworld, said: "The lending rates are still unacceptably high. They are still substantially above inflation and they (the banks) should bring them down lower.
"There's room to bring them down to around 25 percent because the margins that the banks are making are criminal," Kyriakides said.

Anthony Hawkins, professor of business studies at Harare's University of Zimbabwe, cautioned against further cuts saying they would undermine the Reserve Bank's efforts to curb high money supply growth threatening to refuel inflation.

This week, one of the country's biggest banks, Standard Chartered Zimbabwe, lowered its rate to 28.5 percent while Stanbic Bank eased its own to 29 percent. Other banks are expected to follow suit soon, particularly after the Reserve Bank eased its rediscount rate further on Wednesday to 27 percent.

Commercial banks lowered their minimum lending rates to 30 percent from ranges of between 32 and 33 percent in August, citing falls in money market rates to the lower 20s from around 29 percent in January and prospects of lower annual inflation.
The banks pre-empted the central Reserve Bank which later slackened its key rediscount rate to 27.5 percent from 29.5 percent, a level which it had maintained since November 1994.
The southern African country's annual inflation was this week pegged at 20.6 percent, up from a three-year-low of 17.7 percent in August.

"The lower lending rates mean an easing off of the financial mobilisation problems we in industry have been experiencing for the last five years," said Edmore Tobaiwa, senior economist of the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce.
"But the banks should bring down their rates further for them to be of significant benefit to us," Tobaiwa told Reuters.
Zimbabwe's money supply growth has remained stubbornly above the target of 22 percent per year the bank was aiming for in the first five years of Western-backed economic reforms which ended in 1995.

Money and stock market analyst and columnist Nigel Chanakira said by cutting further the benchmark rate at which it lends to financial institutions, the Reserve Bank was being led down a "cul-de-sac" by the government of President Robert Mugabe, who has been echoing private sector complaints about high interest rates.
"As goes the proverbial saying, 'you can't have your cake and eat it', neither can you reduce interest rates and simultaneously money supply and inflation," Chanakira said.
